To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the propagation of chaos for the classical mean-field dynamics can be optimally quantified in the sense that all cumulants are bounded by a power of the mean-field parameter, that the optimal bound is of order 1/√N, and that this result can be rigorously established via a novel non-hierachical approach based on Glauber calculus.

we rigorously prove a propagation of chaos result for the classical mean-field dynamics in the large particle regime, and that we show that the mean field limit of the BBGKY hierachy can be justified on the mean field time scale, which is the optimal timescale for this problem.

(i) the propagation of chaos is optimal in the mean-field scaling, (ii) the Bogolyubv corrections to mean field are quantitatively correct, and (iii) the Lenard– Balescu limit holds in the mean-field setting, away from equilibrium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mathematical foundations of statistical physics, and we believe that our methods are also of interest to the wider mathematical community.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the mean field dynamics in the regime of long-range interaction and large particle number is well approximated by a system of independent particles, with the mean field as an optimal approximation of the one-particle distribution.
the BBGKY approach is not only mathematically correct, but also mathematically useful.

, for a system of classical mean-field particles, the propagation of chaos is optimal in the following sense: the many-body correlations are exponentially decaying in the particle number and, in the mean field regime, they are exponentially small in time.

, in the classical mean-field dynamics, we are able to rigorously quantify the size of chaos in terms of cumulants of the empirical measure.

we rigorously establish the mean-field dynamics in terms of a hierarchy of stochastic equations for correlation functions, which is a crucial ingredient for the derivation of the Vlasov–Poisson equation from classical particles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Glauber stochastic calculus is a powerful tool for analyzing the mean-field dynamics of classical many-body systems.

, for a wide class of initial correlations, the dynamics of the classical mean-field limit is well approximated by the dynamics of an i.i.d. system of mean-field particles, and the error of this approximation can be controlled in terms of the initial data.
the Glauber calculus is a powerful and flexible tool to analyze the mean-field dynamics of many-particle systems.
